D.comparison: structured permission spectrum and permissive program-level carve-out

O.outcome_detail: institutional default stance toward student GenAI permission

cells.quote: Despite these shared baselines, institutions diverge in their default stance toward permission. At the restrictive end, the University of Georgia frames AI use as unauthorized assistance unless explicitly authorized, and its graduate guidance prohibits GenAI use in theses and dissertations unless specifically approved (University of Georgia Academic Honesty n.d.; University of Georgia Graduate School n.d.). Ohio State adopts a similar default in its standard syllabus guidance, stating that GenAI tools should not be used unless the instructor authorizes them (Ohio State University Teaching & Learning Resource Center n.d.). Princeton illustrates another restrictive boundary through academic-support rules that limit the use of non-Princeton tutoring resources, including AI tutoring bots, while also providing faculty with sample policy language that ranges from prohibition to permission with acknowledgment (Princeton University 2025; Princeton University McGraw Center for Teaching & Learning n.d.). Other institutions present structured permission spectra rather than a single default, such as UC Berkeley’s course-policy options and UC San Diego’s syllabus guidance (University of California, Berkeley Research, Teaching, and Learning 2025; University of California, San Diego 2025). At the permissive end, Stanford Graduate School of Business creates a program-level carve-out for MBA/MSx take-home work, where instructors may not ban student AI use for take-home assignments and exams but may regulate disclosure and responsible use (Stanford Graduate School of Business Teaching and Learning Hub 2025).

For learning tasks imposing a low cognitive load, learners working either individually or collaboratively had sufficient cognitive capacity to process all information by themselves. Hence, inter-individual communication and coordination of information were unnecessary and resulted in transaction costs that were higher than the benefits of distributing the cognitive load across group members during the collaborative learning process.
